opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the biggest shifts is that historically, robot hardware was designed to compensate for the fact that we didn't have very good intelligence. If your controller is brittle, if it can't handle uncertainty, then you need the hardware to be extremely precise, extremely stiff, extremely repeatable. That's why classic industrial arms are these heavy, expensive machines with very accurate encoders and gearboxes: the whole system was built so that you could replay a trajectory open-loop and it would land in exactly the same place every time.

Once you have learned controllers that close the loop through perception, and that can correct for errors on the fly the way people do, a lot of that precision becomes unnecessary. Humans aren't precise machines. Our joints are sloppy, our proprioception is pretty noisy, and yet we're incredibly dexterous because we're constantly using feedback. If the intelligence is good enough, you can get away with much cheaper, lighter, more compliant hardware, and the learned policy just makes up for the imperfections. We've seen this already with fairly low-cost arms doing surprisingly delicate tasks like folding laundry, because the model is reacting to what it sees rather than relying on the arm being perfect.

So I think the design question changes from "how do we make this hardware precise enough for our controller" to "how do we make hardware that is cheap, robust, safe around people, and easy to deploy at scale," because scale is really what drives the data flywheel. If you can put many robots out in the world, you get much more diverse experience, and that diversity matters more than the precision of any individual unit.

There's also a second-order effect. If you have a general-purpose model that can control many different embodiments, then hardware designers get a lot more freedom. You don't need to write a new control stack from scratch every time you change the morphology. You can try a different gripper or a different arm configuration, collect some data, and the model can adapt. That lowers the cost of hardware experimentation, and I think we'll see much more variety in robot bodies as a result, rather than everyone converging on one standard form.

I'd add one caveat: I don't think this means hardware stops mattering. Things like good sensing, especially touch, and reliability over thousands of hours of operation are still very important. But the emphasis moves away from precision and toward robustness, affordability, and producing lots of useful data.

r001.rationale: The response says cheaper, lighter, less precise hardware can still perform well, but it does not propose finding the minimum hardware that preserves functionality.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says feedback through perception and learned controllers can correct errors and compensate for imprecise hardware.

r003.rationale: It predicts more variety in robot bodies, including different grippers and arm configurations, rather than convergence on one standard form.

r004.rationale: It says models that work across embodiments make hardware experimentation easier, but does not connect that innovation to tailoring hardware for particular niches.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is that it should change it a lot more than it has so far. Historically, robot hardware has been designed around the limitations of the software. If you look at an industrial arm, it's incredibly rigid, incredibly precise, very repeatable, and that's because the control systems we had basically needed the world to be predictable. You wanted a machine that would do exactly the same thing a million times, and all the intelligence was in the human who programmed the trajectory.

Once you have learning-based systems, that whole calculus flips. The thing that learning is good at is dealing with variability, dealing with imprecision, adapting to the particular situation. So you no longer need the hardware to be perfect. You can actually trade precision for other things: cost, compliance, safety, robustness, speed. A hand that is a little bit floppy and inexpensive, that a learned policy can figure out how to use, might be much more useful than a very expensive, very precise hand that's hard to manufacture and breaks when it hits something.

The other big shift, and I think this is underappreciated, is that the bottleneck is now data. So the question I would ask of any hardware design is: does this platform make it easier or harder to collect lots of experience? Is it cheap enough that you can have hundreds of them? Is it robust enough that it can run for thousands of hours without someone babysitting it? Can it recover on its own when it falls over or jams? Those properties matter a lot more now than, say, shaving another tenth of a millimeter off the repeatability spec. In some sense you want to design robots the way you'd design an experiment, with the data flywheel in mind from day one.

And then there's a more speculative version of this, which is that eventually the AI should be in the loop on the design itself. Right now the hardware is designed by people, and then we train a policy on it, and if it turns out some joint is in the wrong place, well, too bad. But there's no fundamental reason those have to be separate. If you can simulate and learn fast enough, you can co-optimize the morphology and the controller together. I don't think we're quite there in a practical sense, but I think that's where it goes.

The one caution I'd add is that there's a temptation to say, "the learning will take care of everything, so hardware doesn't matter." That's wrong. Hardware still sets the ceiling on what's physically possible, and good sensing in particular, like tactile sensing, makes the learning problem dramatically easier. So it's not that hardware becomes less important. It's that the criteria for what counts as good hardware change completely.

r001.rationale: It says hardware can trade precision for cost, safety, and robustness, but does not propose finding the minimum hardware that still preserves good functionality.

r002.rationale: It explains that learning based policies can handle imprecision and variability, including using a somewhat floppy, inexpensive hand, conveying that learned control can compensate for imperfect hardware.

r003.rationale: It does not predict diverse robot hardware forms or reject convergence on a universal mechanical design.

r004.rationale: It discusses co-optimizing morphology and control, but does not connect hardware tailored to niches with capable AI that works across different robots.

astra-6.text:
I think it should make us reconsider how much of the intelligence we’re putting into the mechanical design. Traditionally, if you want a robot to do a particular task reliably, you can make the learning or control problem easier by carefully engineering the hardware. You build a gripper that fits the object, or a mechanism that constrains the motion in just the right way. That’s a very sensible approach when the software has limited capabilities.

But as the software gets better, the tradeoff changes. You might prefer hardware that’s less specialized, that can do a wider variety of things, even if controlling it is more difficult. A human hand is a good example: it’s tremendously versatile, but it’s certainly not the easiest thing to write a controller for. If learning can handle more of that complexity, then that versatility becomes much more valuable.

The other thing I would emphasize is robustness. For learning, you don’t just want a robot that can perform an impressive demonstration. You want a robot that can operate for a long time, make mistakes, and keep collecting experience without someone having to repair it. A somewhat less precise robot that can survive a lot of interaction might actually be a better platform than a very precise, fragile one.

So I think the hardware question becomes: what kind of body gives a learning system the best opportunity to acquire useful skills? That’s a different objective from designing a machine to execute a particular motion perfectly.

r001.rationale: It favors versatile, robust hardware for learning, but does not propose finding the minimum hardware that preserves good functionality.

r002.rationale: It says learning can handle more control complexity, but does not state that feedback compensates for imprecise hardware.

r003.rationale: It contrasts specialized hardware with more versatile designs, but does not predict that robot hardware will take diverse forms instead of converging on a universal humanlike design.

r004.rationale: It discusses adapting hardware to learning, but does not argue that AI usable across different robots will enable niche-specific hardware innovation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that we should design the hardware and the learning system together. Traditionally, you build a robot that you know how to control, and that pushes you toward very precise actuators, very rigid mechanisms, and very accurate sensing. You’re making the hardware compensate for limitations in your ability to write the software.

With learning, you can potentially make a different tradeoff. Maybe the mechanism can be less precise, or have more compliance, because the controller can learn to deal with those properties. That could let you build something cheaper, more robust, or safer around people. But learning doesn’t eliminate physical constraints. If your hand can’t exert enough force, no amount of intelligence will make it pick up a heavy object.

The other thing I would emphasize is iteration. We tend to ask, ‘What is the best possible robot?’ But if the robot is going to learn from experience, you also have to ask, ‘How many of these can I build, and how much experience can they collect?’ A somewhat less capable robot that you can deploy in large numbers might ultimately be more useful than an exquisite machine that you can only afford to build once.

So I would optimize for a platform that has the physical capabilities you need, but is also inexpensive, reliable, easy to repair, and able to collect useful data. The hardware is part of the learning process.

r001.rationale: The response proposes less precise, cheaper hardware that can still meet needed physical capabilities, but does not clearly propose finding the minimum hardware that preserves good functionality.

r002.rationale: It says a learned controller can deal with hardware properties such as reduced precision, communicating that learning can compensate for imprecise hardware.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that robots will take diverse forms or reject convergence on a universal mechanical person.

r004.rationale: It discusses inexpensive, scalable robots, but does not say that AI usable across different robots will spur hardware tailored to particular niches.
